name: Gin & Tonic
notes: Build in the glass over ice, add tonic last, one gentle lift with the barspoon. Stirring hard kills the carbonation.

name: Vodka Soda
notes: The template for every well highball: 2 oz spirit, top with mixer, citrus wedge. Learn this ratio and a dozen drinks come free.

name: Screwdriver
notes: Vodka and OJ. Add a splash of Galliano on top and it is a Harvey Wallbanger.

name: Cuba Libre
notes: A Rum & Coke becomes a Cuba Libre the moment fresh lime goes in. If a guest asks for the real thing, squeeze the lime.

name: Whiskey Ginger
notes: Ginger ale, not ginger beer. Swap in ginger beer and lime and you have built a Mule.

name: Jack & Coke
notes: Called by brand, so pour the brand. Substituting another whiskey without saying so is how you lose a regular.

name: Cape Codder
notes: Also ordered as a Vodka Cranberry. Add grapefruit and it is a Sea Breeze; add pineapple and it is a Bay Breeze.

name: Sea Breeze
notes: Sea = grapefruit. Bay = pineapple. Same vodka-cranberry base, and mixing them up is the single most common breeze mistake.

name: Bay Breeze
notes: Bay = pineapple. Drop the cranberry entirely and it is a Pineapple Screwdriver, not a breeze.

name: Tom Collins
notes: A gin sour lengthened with soda. Shake the first three, strain over fresh ice, then top. Never shake the soda.

name: Paloma
notes: Mexico's actual everyday tequila drink, far more common there than the Margarita. Squeeze of salt in the build, not just on the rim.

name: Dark 'n' Stormy
notes: Build the ginger beer and lime first, then float the dark rum on top so it storms down through the glass. The name is trademarked to Gosling's.

name: Moscow Mule
notes: Ginger beer, not ginger ale. Swap the vodka for any spirit and it stays a mule: bourbon makes a Kentucky, tequila a Mexican, gin a London.

name: Kentucky Mule
notes: Proof that the mule is a template, not a recipe. Same build, bourbon in the vodka's place.

name: Margarita
notes: 2:1:1 tequila, triple sec, lime. Shake hard with ice, strain into a salt-rimmed rocks glass over fresh ice. Swap triple sec for agave + more lime and it's a Tommy's Margarita.

name: Daiquiri
notes: 2:1:0.75, the sour ratio in its purest form. Shake hard and long — this drink is about the shake, not the ingredients. Add pureed strawberry or peach and it becomes a fruit daiquiri.

name: Whiskey Sour
notes: With egg white, dry-shake first (no ice) to build foam, then shake again with ice. Skip the dry shake and the foam never forms.

name: Amaretto Sour
notes: Less simple syrup than a whiskey sour since amaretto is already sweet. Same egg-white dry-shake technique if used.

name: Gimlet
notes: Traditionally Rose's lime cordial, not fresh lime juice — that's what separates it from a gin sour. A modern version uses fresh lime plus simple syrup instead.

name: Sidecar
notes: A brandy Margarita, essentially — same shake-and-strain structure with cognac instead of tequila and lemon instead of lime.

name: Cosmopolitan
garnish: Lime wheel or flamed orange peel
notes: The cranberry is for color and a hint of tartness, not to dominate — go easy on it or the drink turns into juice.

name: Lemon Drop
notes: A vodka sour with a sugared rim. Also served as a shot — see the shots section for the smaller-format version.

name: Pisco Sour
garnish: Three dashes of bitters drawn through the foam
notes: Always dry-shake the egg white first. The bitters go on top of the foam as a garnish pattern, not mixed in.

name: Bee's Knees
notes: Honey syrup is 1:1 honey and hot water, stirred until dissolved — straight honey won't incorporate in a cold shake.

name: Old Fashioned
notes: The original cocktail template: spirit, sugar, bitters, ice. Muddle a sugar cube with bitters if no syrup is on hand, then build and stir.

name: Sazerac
notes: Rinse a chilled rocks glass with absinthe and dump the excess before stirring the rest and straining in — served up, no ice in the glass.

name: Rusty Nail
notes: Just two spirits built over ice and stirred briefly in the glass. No syrup, no bitters — the Drambuie brings its own sweetness.

name: Dry Martini
notes: Stirred, never shaken — no juice or dairy means shaking only adds unwanted dilution and ice shards. "Dry" means less vermouth; ask before assuming a ratio.

name: Dirty Martini
notes: "Dirty" specifies olive brine added to the stir. Ask how dirty — more brine for guests who want it cloudier and saltier.

name: Gibson
notes: Identical build to a Dry Martini; the only difference is the garnish — onions instead of an olive or twist.

name: Vesper
notes: The one martini-family drink that's shaken, per Bond's own order — no vermouth, Lillet Blanc stands in its place.

name: Espresso Martini
notes: Shake hard and long — the foam cap on top comes entirely from the shake, there's no egg white or cream involved.

name: Manhattan
notes: 2:1 whiskey to sweet vermouth, stirred and strained up. The whiskey-forward sibling of the Negroni's equal-parts build.

name: Rob Roy
notes: A Manhattan built with scotch instead of rye or bourbon — same 2:1 ratio, same stir and strain.

name: Negroni
notes: Equal parts, stirred, served over one large cube. No citrus in the mix, so it's always stirred rather than shaken.

name: Boulevardier
notes: A Negroni with bourbon standing in for the gin, and slightly whiskey-forward rather than dead equal parts.

name: Vieux Carré
notes: New Orleans' answer to the Manhattan — five ingredients, still just built by stirring everything over ice and straining.

name: Aperol Spritz
notes: 3-2-1: prosecco, Aperol, soda, built in that order over ice so the bubbles aren't beaten flat by pouring spirit on top of them.

name: Mimosa
notes: Equal parts, poured gently to preserve carbonation. Pour the juice first so the sparkling wine's fizz doesn't get knocked down by the pour.

name: Bellini
notes: Purée goes in the flute first, then top slowly with prosecco and give one gentle stir to combine without losing the fizz.

name: French 75
notes: Shake the gin, lemon, and syrup, strain into the flute, then top with champagne — the only spritz-family drink built on a proper shaken sour base.

name: Kir Royale
notes: Cassis first, then top with champagne. Swap champagne for still white wine and drop the "Royale" and it's a plain Kir.

name: Mai Tai
garnish: Mint sprig and spent lime shell
notes: Shake with crushed ice and dump the whole thing into the glass (do not strain). Orgeat is the almond syrup that gives it the signature nutty backbone.

name: Piña Colada
notes: Blended, not shaken — everything goes in the blender with crushed ice until smooth and pourable.

name: Painkiller
notes: Shake and pour unstrained over crushed ice. The nutmeg grated fresh on top is non-negotiable for this one.

name: Hurricane
notes: Two rums, shaken hard and poured into a hurricane glass over fresh ice — invented at Pat O'Brien's in New Orleans.

name: Jungle Bird
notes: The rare tiki drink built around a bittering agent — the Campari cuts the pineapple sweetness instead of just adding more fruit.

name: Mojito
notes: Press mint gently to release oils — do not shred it, that releases bitter chlorophyll. Build in the glass, top with soda, swizzle rather than stir.

name: Caipirinha
notes: Muddle whole lime wedges with sugar directly in the glass before adding cachaça and crushed ice — no juicing, the muddle does the work.

name: Bloody Mary
notes: Roll (pour between two glasses) rather than shake — shaking makes the tomato juice foam and separate.

name: Long Island Iced Tea
notes: Five spirits at a half ounce each, shaken with lemon and syrup, strained over ice, topped with a splash of cola for color. No cola-heavy pour — it should taste like a sour, not a soda.

name: Mint Julep
notes: Muddle mint with syrup only (no bourbon yet) to avoid bruising, then pack the cup with crushed ice and pour bourbon over, swizzling until the cup frosts.

name: White Russian
notes: Build vodka and coffee liqueur over ice, then float the cream gently on top by pouring over the back of a spoon rather than stirring it in.

name: Mudslide
notes: Shaken and strained rather than built, so all four ingredients fully combine instead of layering like a White Russian.

name: Brandy Alexander
notes: Shake hard with ice to aerate the cream, then strain up. Grate nutmeg over the foam right before serving.

name: Kamikaze
notes: Equal parts, shaken hard with ice and strained into a shot glass — a shot-format Margarita relative without the salt or tequila.

name: Lemon Drop Shot
notes: Shake and strain into a sugar-rimmed shot glass, served with a sugar-coated lemon wedge to bite after.

name: Washington Apple
notes: Shake with ice and strain — the whiskey, apple schnapps, and cranberry balance is what makes it taste like a candy apple.

name: Green Tea Shot
notes: Contains no actual tea — the whiskey and peach schnapps combination just turns the color of green tea when shaken and strained.

name: B-52
notes: Layered by density, heaviest first: coffee liqueur, then Irish cream, then orange liqueur poured slowly over the back of a barspoon so each layer floats distinct.

name: Michelada
notes: Rim the glass with salt and Tajín, build the seasonings and lime first, then top slowly with beer to avoid excess foam.

name: Irish Coffee
notes: Pre-heat the mug with hot water first. Whip the cream just to soft, pourable peaks and float it over the back of a spoon so it sits on top rather than mixing in.

name: Aviation
notes: Crème de violette should be a whisper, not a flood — too much turns the drink purple and perfumey instead of pale grey-blue.

name: Clover Club
notes: Dry-shake with the egg white first to build foam, then shake again with ice — same two-step technique as a Whiskey Sour.

name: Last Word
notes: Equal parts of four ingredients — the easiest classic to remember and the hardest to keep in stock, since green Chartreuse is the one bottle every bar runs out of.

name: Corpse Reviver No. 2
notes: "Four of these taken in swift succession will unrevive the corpse again" — Harry Craddock's own warning. The absinthe rinse coats the glass and gets dumped, never measured in.

name: Paper Plane
notes: Equal parts, a 2010s cocktail already inducted into the modern canon. Amaro Nonino specifically is not swappable without changing the drink noticeably.

name: Southside
notes: Mint is muddled gently, then shaken with the rest and double-strained so no leaf fragments make it into the glass.

name: Bramble
notes: Shake the gin, lemon, and syrup, strain over crushed ice, then drizzle the blackberry liqueur on top so it bleeds through the drink rather than mixing in.

name: White Lady
notes: Essentially a gin Sidecar. Some versions add egg white for texture — dry-shake first if you do.

name: Between the Sheets
notes: Equal parts of three spirits plus lemon — a Sidecar with rum added, and stronger than the short ingredient list suggests.

name: Jack Rose
notes: Use real pomegranate grenadine, not corn-syrup bar syrup — both the color and the flavor fall flat with the fake stuff.

name: Ward 8
notes: A Whiskey Sour with orange juice added and grenadine standing in for simple syrup.

name: Hemingway Daiquiri
notes: Also called the Papa Doble. No added sugar — the maraschino carries the sweetness against tart grapefruit and lime.

name: Mary Pickford
notes: Named for the silent-film star. Shake hard so the pineapple juice froths properly before straining up.

name: Bacardi Cocktail
notes: Historically required by a 1936 court ruling to be made with Bacardi brand rum specifically — a Daiquiri with grenadine in place of syrup.

name: El Presidente
notes: Stirred, not shaken — this is a rum Martini relative, not a sour, even though the ingredient list looks sweet on paper.

name: Casino
notes: One of the oldest gin sours on record, predating the Aviation by decades.

name: Twentieth Century
notes: The crème de cacao is used dry, not as a dessert note — this reads as a bright, citrus-forward gin sour despite the chocolate liqueur.

name: Chrysanthemum
notes: No base spirit at all — vermouth is the base, which makes this a good low-ABV stirred option when a guest wants something lighter.

name: Bijou
notes: Equal parts, named for the "jewel" colors of its three spirits — gin (diamond), vermouth (ruby), Chartreuse (emerald).

name: Widow's Kiss
notes: Two liqueurs plus applejack, all stirred — deceptively strong for how sweet it tastes on the way down.

name: Remember the Maine
notes: A Manhattan variation named for the USS Maine, with cherry liqueur and an absinthe rinse standing in for plain bitters.

name: Blood and Sand
notes: Equal parts of four ingredients — shaken, not stirred, because the orange juice needs the aeration.

name: Monkey Gland
notes: Named (crudely) for a 1920s rejuvenation fad. The anise dash is barely perceptible but rounds the orange and gin together.

name: Corpse Reviver No. 1
notes: The stirred, spirit-forward sibling of the more famous No. 2 — meant as an actual hangover remedy, not a citrus-forward sour.

name: Pink Lady
notes: Dry-shake the egg white first, same technique as a Whiskey Sour, for the drink's signature pale pink foam.

name: Caipiroska
notes: The Caipirinha's vodka-based cousin — same muddle technique, cachaça swapped out for vodka.

name: Caipirissima
notes: Same build as a Caipirinha with white rum standing in for cachaça.

name: Ti' Punch
notes: From the French Caribbean — built to the guest's own taste at the table, with the lime squeezed (not juiced) directly into the glass.

name: Batida
notes: Brazilian blended drink, endlessly variable — swap in puréed fruit like passion fruit or mango for the coconut and it's still a Batida.

name: Pisco Punch
notes: A Gold Rush-era San Francisco classic. Pineapple gum syrup (pineapple-infused syrup with gum arabic) is the ingredient nobody has on hand, so infuse it ahead of service.

name: Rum Punch
notes: "One of sour, two of sweet, three of strong, four of weak" is the rhyme bartenders use to freehand this without a recipe card.

name: Planter's Punch
notes: An older, simpler cousin of the modern Rum Punch — built around bitters instead of extra juice.

name: Queen's Park Swizzle
notes: Built and swizzled with a swizzle stick spun between the palms rather than shaken, packing the glass with crushed ice as you go.

name: Corn 'n' Oil
notes: From Barbados — built directly in the glass, no shaking, so the blackstrap rum's heaviness sinks through the drink like "oil."

name: Piscola
notes: Chile's most-ordered drink by a wide margin — as simple as a Jack & Coke, just with pisco in place of whiskey.

name: Cantarito
notes: Named for the small clay cup it's traditionally served in — a highball glass is the practical substitute behind most bars.

name: Ranch Water
notes: A West Texas staple, traditionally built right in the mineral-water bottle with the tequila and lime added to it.

name: Batanga
notes: Stir with a long knife blade, per its inventor's own signature move — a barspoon works fine if one isn't handy.

name: Chilcano
notes: Peru's answer to the Moscow Mule — same shape, pisco and ginger ale standing in for vodka and ginger beer.

name: Rum Swizzle
notes: Bermuda's national drink — swizzled with crushed ice until the glass frosts over, the same technique as a Queen's Park Swizzle.

name: Suffering Bastard
notes: Invented in Cairo as a hangover remedy for British troops — gin and brandy together is unusual, and that's the point.

name: Fish House Punch
notes: A colonial Philadelphia punch dating to the 1730s, traditionally batched by the bowl — this app's servings scaler is the fast way to size it up for a party.

name: Trinidad Sour
notes: Bitters as the base spirit, not a seasoning — 1.5 oz of Angostura looks like a typo the first time you read the recipe, but it isn't.

name: Doctor Funk
notes: Named for the missionary doctor said to have invented it in Samoa — the anise dash is a signature, not an optional garnish.

name: Hotel Nacional Special
notes: From Havana's Hotel Nacional. Apricot liqueur (not brandy proper) is what separates this from a plain rum-and-pineapple.

name: Penicillin
notes: Shake the blended Scotch base, strain over ice, then float the smoky Islay Scotch on top so you smell it before you taste it.

name: Gold Rush
notes: A Whiskey Sour with honey instead of simple syrup and no egg white — sometimes called a bourbon on-the-rocks Bee's Knees.

name: Naked & Famous
notes: Equal parts, a smoky answer to the Last Word — built the same way, with mezcal and Aperol standing in for gin and green Chartreuse.

name: Oaxaca Old Fashioned
notes: An Old Fashioned built on tequila with mezcal added for smoke — the mezcal is a seasoning here, not a co-base.

name: Kentucky Buck
notes: A Kentucky Mule with lemon and bitters added — the bitters are what keep it from just being bourbon-and-ginger.

name: Tommy's Margarita
notes: Drop the triple sec, add agave — this became the house Margarita at most serious cocktail bars for a reason.

name: Brooklyn
notes: Amer Picon is nearly impossible to find in the US; most bars substitute another orange-forward amaro and adjust to taste.

name: Greenpoint
notes: A Brooklyn made rounder and easier to stock — yellow Chartreuse and extra bitters instead of Amer Picon.

name: Elder Fashioned
notes: St-Germain elderflower liqueur stands in for the sugar, giving a lighter, floral take on the Old Fashioned template.

name: Gin Gin Mule
notes: Shake the gin, lime, syrup, and mint first, strain over fresh ice, then top with ginger beer — more cocktail than the average mule.

name: Hugo Spritz
notes: Prosecco and elderflower liqueur built the same way as an Aperol Spritz — lighter and less bitter, popular across German-speaking Europe.

name: Whiskey Smash
notes: Whole lemon wedges are muddled directly in the shaker along with the mint, giving more body than a plain lemon-juice sour.

name: Mezcal Negroni
notes: Swap the gin in a Negroni for mezcal and the equal-parts build stays identical — just smokier.

name: Cable Car
notes: A spiced-rum Sidecar, essentially — the cinnamon-sugar rim is what makes it taste like the drink rather than a generic rum sour.

name: Final Ward
notes: The Last Word rebuilt with rye and lemon instead of gin and lime — same equal-parts structure, different backbone.

name: Bitter Giuseppe
notes: A lower-proof spritz built around bitter amaro and vermouth instead of a base spirit — pours easily as a session aperitif.

name: Air Mail
notes: Shake the rum, lime, and honey, strain into the flute, then top with champagne — a rum-based sibling of the French 75.

name: Pegu Club
notes: Named for the officers' club in colonial Rangoon — two different bitters is deliberate, not a typo.

name: Death in the Afternoon
notes: Hemingway's own recipe: "pour one jigger absinthe, add iced champagne until it attains the proper opalescent milkiness." Pour the champagne slowly — absinthe louches on contact.

name: Kingston Negroni
notes: The gin in a Negroni swapped for a funky, high-ester Jamaican rum — pick one with real character or the swap doesn't register.

name: Buttery Nipple
notes: Layer by density — butterscotch schnapps first, Irish cream floated on top over the back of a barspoon.

name: Alabama Slammer
notes: Shaken with ice and strained — also served full-size over ice in a highball as a "tall" Slammer.

name: Jäger Bomb
notes: Drop the chilled Jägermeister shot glass-and-all into the energy drink and slam immediately — the point is the reaction, not sipping.

name: Red Headed Slut
notes: Shaken quickly with ice and strained — a fruitier, sweeter counterpoint to a straight Jägermeister shot.

name: Slippery Nipple
notes: Sambuca poured first, Irish cream floated over a barspoon — the same layering technique as a Buttery Nipple with different liqueurs.

name: Mind Eraser
notes: Built as three distinct layers over ice and drunk fast through a straw from the bottom up — that's the "eraser" part.

name: Cement Mixer
notes: A novelty shot — the lime juice curdles the Irish cream instantly in the mouth into a chewable lump. Warn first-timers.

name: Duck Fart
notes: Coffee liqueur first, Irish cream next, whisky floated last — three clean layers if poured slowly over a spoon.

name: Surfer on Acid
notes: Shaken and strained — the pineapple and coconut round off the Jägermeister's bite more than most mixers manage.

name: Three Wise Men
notes: Three whiskeys, no mixer — a bar-brand-recognition shot more than a crafted recipe.

name: Woo Woo
notes: Shaken and strained; poured over ice in a rocks glass instead, it's the same drink as a full cocktail, just bigger.

name: Melon Ball
notes: Midori is the whole flavor here — it should taste distinctly of honeydew melon, not just look green.

name: Blow Job
notes: Built, then topped with a cap of whipped cream — served without hands, a novelty-bar staple.

name: Chocolate Cake Shot
notes: Shaken and strained, then chased with a sugar-coated lemon wedge — the sugar and citrus combination is what actually tastes like cake, not the shot itself.

name: Pickleback
notes: Two shots, back to back — whiskey first, brine immediately after. The brine's acidity and salt scrub the whiskey burn off the palate.

name: Zombie
notes: Three rums is standard here, not excess — the layered rum character is the entire point, and it's genuinely strong despite tasting like fruit juice.

name: Scorpion Bowl
notes: Built to share — this is the drink the app's batch scaler exists for. Bump servings to size it up for the table rather than remixing the ratio by hand.

name: Navy Grog
notes: Three rums again, but drier and less sweet than a Zombie — grapefruit stands in for extra sugar.

name: Fog Cutter
notes: Three base spirits plus a sherry float — famously strong enough that Trader Vic warned "let it get to you, quietly."

name: Three Dots and a Dash
garnish: Three brandied cherries and a pineapple spear
notes: Named for its garnish — Morse code for "V." The fruit skewer isn't optional; it's the whole joke.

name: Beachcomber
notes: A tiki drink served up in a coupe rather than over ice — closer in structure to a Daiquiri variation than to a Zombie.

name: Missionary's Downfall
notes: Blended with crushed ice until slushy — one of the few tiki drinks built around mint instead of falernum or orgeat.

name: Saturn
notes: An IBA official cocktail — a gin base is unusual for tiki, since most of the category runs on rum.

name: Test Pilot
notes: A Donn Beach original — the overproof float on top is what gives it more kick than a Mai Tai.

name: 151 Swizzle
notes: Swizzled, not shaken — the crushed ice does the dilution as you spin the swizzle stick, since a full shake would over-dilute this strong a pour.

name: Bahama Mama
notes: A beach-bar staple built for volume — easy to batch by the pitcher for a group.

name: Blue Hawaii
notes: The blue curaçao is entirely for color — flavor-wise it's an orange liqueur, so don't expect it to taste "blue."

name: Chi-Chi
notes: A Piña Colada with vodka instead of rum — otherwise an identical blend.

name: Singapore Sling
notes: From Raffles Hotel in Singapore — nine ingredients is not a typo, and skipping any one of the liqueurs changes the drink noticeably.

name: Jet Pilot
notes: A Test Pilot relative with grapefruit and cinnamon added — another three-rum build where the overproof float carries the finish.

name: Americano
notes: Equal parts Campari and sweet vermouth, topped with soda — the Negroni's predecessor and, at half the ABV, still the better daytime order.

name: John Collins
notes: Identical build to a Tom Collins with whiskey standing in for gin — same shake-strain-top structure.

name: Horse's Neck
notes: The peel is the entire point of the drink's name — cut one long continuous spiral and drape it over the rim into the glass, don't just drop in a wedge.

name: Shirley Temple
notes: The standard answer for a non-drinking guest or a kid at the bar — build the grenadine first so it sinks and swirls when stirred at the table.

name: Arnold Palmer
notes: Half lemonade, half iced tea, named for the golfer who ordered it that way — add vodka or whiskey and it becomes a "John Daly."

name: Salty Dog
notes: Identical to a Greyhound with a salted rim added — the rim is the only difference between the two names.

name: Greyhound
notes: No salt rim — add one and it becomes a Salty Dog, nothing else about the build changes.

name: Gin Fizz
notes: Shake the first three hard, strain into the glass, then top with soda — a Tom Collins built up rather than long over fresh ice from the start.

name: Ramos Gin Fizz
notes: Shake for a full two minutes minimum, longer than any other drink in this deck — the extended shake is what builds the signature marshmallow-thick foam.

name: Sloe Gin Fizz
notes: Sloe gin is a liqueur, not a gin — sweeter and fruitier, so this fizz needs less added syrup than a plain Gin Fizz.

name: Pimm's Cup
garnish: Cucumber ribbon, mint, orange and strawberry slices
notes: The fruit garnish is heavy by design — a proper Pimm's Cup is half garnish, and guests pick through it as they drink.

name: Shandy
notes: Equal parts beer and lemonade, called a Radler in Germany — same drink under a different name.

name: Snakebite
notes: Equal parts lager and hard cider, built directly in the glass — ordered as a "diesel" in some UK pubs with a splash of blackcurrant added.

name: Black Velvet
notes: Pour the champagne first, then float the stout slowly over a spoon so the two layer rather than mix — an Irish-pub classic.

name: Tequila Sunrise
notes: Build tequila and orange juice first, then sink the grenadine down a barspoon so it settles at the bottom and rises like a sunrise — never stir it in.

name: Grasshopper
notes: Equal parts of three ingredients, shaken hard to aerate the cream — tastes like a liquid thin-mint cookie.

name: Golden Cadillac
notes: Same equal-parts structure as a Grasshopper, with Galliano's vanilla-anise standing in for the mint.

name: Pink Squirrel
notes: Crème de noyaux is almond-flavored and naturally pink, which is the entire source of the drink's name and color.

name: Alexander
notes: The gin original that the Brandy Alexander later replaced with brandy — grate nutmeg over the foam the same way.

name: Velvet Hammer
notes: No base spirit — two liqueurs and cream, which makes it deceptively easy to drink for its actual ABV.

name: Nutty Irishman
notes: Built over ice rather than shaken — the two liqueurs already carry enough body without extra aeration.

name: Toasted Almond
notes: Shake and strain over fresh ice — amaretto and coffee liqueur together taste exactly like the drink's name promises.

name: Separator
notes: A lesser-known Brandy Alexander relative built with coffee liqueur instead of crème de cacao.

name: Chocolate Martini
notes: Despite the name it's a cream cocktail, not a true Martini — there's no vermouth anywhere in it.
